-- prelude

This is the contents of the post
I wrote to start a thread on 
>>discourse.atmosphere.community|
https://discourse.atmosphere.community>>
to start a discussion about NeoDoc.


-- tldr

I designed a content format to replace 
Markdown. It lets you add attributes to 
content. You can do all kinds of stuff 
with them without having to mess with HTML.

I've been using it on my site for the 
past few years. I think it would work 
great as an interoperable content format 
for the atmosphere (the goal being to help 
ensure the stuff we make is as portable 
as possible). So, I'm offering it up.

You can learn more about it at
>>neodoc.style|https://neodoc.style/>>


-- title

A Community Pitch

Hey folks,

I've been on Bluesky for a bit. It's only 
recently that I learned enough about the 
Atmosphere to start getting what it's about. 
I don't remember the last time I was this 
excited about new tech. 

I saw standard.site kicking around a couple 
weeks ago. I jumped on it^^1^^. It's the kind 
of stuff I dream about^^2^^. 

One thing the leaflet post^^3^^ on standard.site 
mentions is it's not a content standard. 
The only post^^4^^ I've seen on a content 
standard for the Atmosphere has to do with 
a wordpress lexicon for publishing HTML. 

I submit that HTML could work as a standardized 
content format. It's a battle tested standard 
that renders natively in browsers without 
modification. There are a couple things to 
recommend against it, though.


-- numbered

1. It's not friendly to writing by hand. 
Unless you're hard-core it's not something 
most folks are into. Tooling would be necessary 
to convert content from plain-text into HTML 
before storage. 

2. It's tough to standardize content types. 
Microformats^^5^^ were an attempt. They never 
took off. That's at least partially because they 
lock the data into the rendering layer. Sure, 
you can do all kinds of things with CSS, but 
you have to set up a parser if you want to use 
the data independently. 


-- p

Markdown is another option. It's easy to learn 
and already has huge market share in the 
developer community. It's great for blog posts, 
but kinda sucks for anything beyond. (I mean,
you can always roll your own HTML, but that
justs add the complexity of dealing with 
HTML on to the handling. 

Markdown also lacks the ability to add 
metadata to content. For example, say you 
to apply a custom style to one of the ``H2`` 
elements on a page. There's no mechanism to 
do that in native Markdown. You have to 
switch to inline HTML.
